title: Quick reference: traffic control numbers
text: MUTCD taper formulas: 40 mph or less, L = W x S squared / 60; 45 mph or more, L = W x S (W = offset in ft, S = speed in mph). Merging taper L; shifting 1/2 L; shoulder 1/3 L; flagger one-lane two-way taper 50 to 100 ft; downstream taper 50 to 100 ft. 12 ft lane at 35 mph: 245 ft; at 55 mph: 660 ft. Advance sign spacing (national Table 6B-1; the road agency decides which streets are low or high speed, and some state manuals set it by mph): urban low speed 100 ft each; urban high speed 350 ft; rural 500 ft; freeway 1,000, 1,500, 2,640 ft. Buffer and flagger distance: 30 mph 200 ft; 35 mph 250 ft; 45 mph 360 ft; 55 mph 495 ft. Cone spacing guidance: taper, speed in mph as feet; tangent, twice that. Check your state standards and MUTCD edition.
source: FHWA MUTCD Part 6 (as summarized)

title: Advance warning signs, flaggers and buffer space
text: Typical advance warning sign spacing (the MUTCD sign spacing table, distances A, B, C between signs): urban low speed 100 ft each (the road agency sets the speed category; some state manuals set it by mph); urban high speed 350 ft; rural 500 ft; expressway and freeway 1,000 / 1,500 / 2,640 ft. Leave a longitudinal buffer space ahead of the work when possible. Flaggers: trained (many states require flagger certification), wearing high-visibility apparel (ANSI 107 Class 2 or 3), using a STOP/SLOW paddle, standing where approaching drivers can see them in time and with an escape route; give the flagger a flagger-ahead sign in advance. Nighttime work needs lighting and retroreflective gear. The permit's traffic control plan governs on that job.
source: FHWA MUTCD 11th Edition Part 6; ANSI/ISEA 107

title: Water main disinfection and bac-T samples (AWWA C651)
text: Keep pipe clean during laying, then disinfect before connecting to the system. AWWA C651 methods: continuous feed (water with at least 25 mg/L free chlorine fills the main, held 24 hours, ending with at least 10 mg/L), tablet (25 mg/L, 24 hours, water above 41 F), or slug (100 mg/L passed through for at least 3 hours). Agency specs can be stronger (Greenbook: 50 to 100 mg/L, 24 hours, 25 mg/L residual). Flush until the water is at system chlorine levels, dechlorinate the flush water before discharge, then take bacteriological (bac-T) samples: two sets that both pass, taken as the spec says (AWWA C651-14: a second set at least 16 hours after the first, or let the main sit 16 hours and take two sets 15 minutes apart; specs written on the 2005 edition say 24 hours apart), or per the agency; all must show no coliform. Don't connect until samples pass, and resample if the main isn't put in service in time.
source: AWWA C651; Greenbook 306-8.9.4

title: Quick reference: water main test numbers
text: Common water main numbers (check your spec, which governs). Hydrostatic test: AWWA C600 per U.S. Pipe, at least 1.25 times working pressure at the high point and 1.5 times at the low point; some utilities use 150 psi or 1.5 times working pressure, others working pressure plus 100 psi; hold at least 2 hours. Allowable make-up water L (gallons per hour) = S x D x square root of P / 148,000; for 1,000 ft of 8 inch at 150 psi, about 0.66 gal/hr. Disinfection (AWWA C651): continuous feed at least 25 mg/L, held 24 hours, at least 10 mg/L remaining; slug at least 100 mg/L for 3 hours; tablet about 25 mg/L for 24 hours. Bac-T samples every 1,200 ft plus end and branches, two consecutive acceptable sets. Flush before chlorinating at 3.0 ft per second or more (AWWA C651-14 Sec. 4.4.2; the 2005 edition said 2.5 ft per second, which is about 390 gpm in 8 inch).
source: AWWA C600 (U.S. Pipe), utility specs, AWWA C651 summary

text: Federal OSHA requires a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring or a shield) in an excavation 5 ft or deeper unless it is entirely in stable rock, and in a shallower one when the competent person sees a cave-in hazard (29 CFR 1926.652). Twenty-one states run their own OSHA plan for private construction crews; a plan must be at least as protective as federal and may be stricter, so on those jobs cite the state rule. What has been checked against the state's own rule text so far (as of 2026-11-20): Washington requires protection at 4 ft and, since June 1, 2026, a written trench work plan and a competent person on site during trench work; California keeps 5 ft and adds a Cal/OSHA permit for excavations 5 ft or deeper that people enter; Michigan uses its own Part 9 (slope or support over 5 ft, with its own angle table); Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon and Utah adopt the federal excavation standard, so 5 ft; Alaska, Kentucky, Minnesota and Tennessee adopt the federal rule and Hawaii, North Carolina and Virginia list no excavation rule of their own (from OSHA's and the agencies' pages, not each state code read line by line), so 5 ft; South Carolina uses the federal text and adds training to the competent person definition. Not yet checked: Indiana, Iowa, Maryland (a state supplement to the federal rule exists and was not read), Vermont and Wyoming; treat federal 5 ft as the floor there and ask the state agency or your safety person whether the plan adds anything. In every state the competent person and your company program decide what protection a trench gets.
title: State OSHA plans and trench protection depth: which rule book applies on your job
topic: State OSHA plans: where trench and confined space rules differ from federal OSHA
source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1); osha.gov/stateplans; Wash. Admin. Code 296-155-657; 8 CCR 341; Mich. Admin. Code R 408.40941; AZ R20-5-601; UT R614-1-4; OR 437-003-0001; NM 11.5.3.9 NMAC; checked 2026-11-20

title: Yellow plastic pipe in the trench wall: natural gas, stop and call
text: A yellow plastic pipe (solid yellow, or black with yellow stripes) uncovered in a trench wall or bottom is almost always a gas line: yellow is the APWA color for gas, oil, steam and petroleum, and polyethylene gas mains and services run from 1/2 inch to 12 inch, sometimes with a tracer wire or yellow warning tape above. Nothing about a photo tells you whether it is live, abandoned or at what pressure; California law says to presume every line is active (Gov Code 4216.4(a)(3)). Stop digging near it, keep the bucket away, do not pull on it, hang on it or use it as a step, and do not try to cut or cap it. If it is not on your ticket, call 811 and the gas operator; if it was marked and you are inside the 24 inch tolerance zone with a machine, you are already outside the one-call law. Any contact, even a scrape of the pipe, is reported to the gas company at once (Gov Code 4216.4(c)(2)); escaping gas is a 911 call first (4216.4(c)(1)). Hissing, smell or dirt blowing: 911, everyone upwind, no ignition sources, no restarting the machine.
topic: Replacement chunks with the words crews type (retrieval fixes)
source: APWA Uniform Color Code; California Government Code 4216.4(a)(3), (c)(1), (c)(2); gas operator guidance

title: Severe bleeding: recognize it and apply direct pressure (Stop the Bleed)
text: Life-threatening bleeding can kill in minutes, before an ambulance reaches a jobsite. Signs: blood spurting or flowing steadily, blood pooling on the ground, clothing or bandages soaking through, a limb partly or fully cut off, or a person confused or passing out while bleeding. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Tell them 'severe bleeding'. Make sure the scene is safe (equipment stopped, out of the trench). 2. Put on gloves if you have them; don't delay long to find them. 3. Find where the blood is coming from. Open or cut clothing to see the wound. 4. Put a clean dressing, gauze or cloth over the wound and press down hard with both hands, using your body weight. 5. Keep pushing without letting up until the bleeding stops or EMS takes over. Do not lift the dressing to check; add more on top if it soaks through. 6. If pressure doesn't stop bleeding from an arm or leg, use a tourniquet. If the wound is deep or in the groin, armpit or neck, pack it. Stop the Bleed offers free or low-cost hands-on courses; take one.
source: Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons), as summarized in Florida DOH Stop the Bleed card

title: Wound packing for deep bleeding wounds
text: Wound packing is the Stop the Bleed method for deep wounds where a tourniquet won't work, such as the groin, armpit, neck or a large deep wound on the body or upper leg. Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Gloves on if available. 2. Expose the wound and find the bleeding. 3. Push hemostatic gauze, plain gauze or the cleanest cloth you have straight into the wound, packing it tightly with your fingers until the wound is full. Keep feeding gauze in until no more fits. 4. Put both hands on top of the packed wound and press down hard with your body weight. 5. Hold firm, steady pressure until the bleeding stops or EMS takes over. The Stop the Bleed course teaches how long to hold; when in doubt, keep holding. 6. Don't pack wounds of the chest or belly that go into the body cavity; just cover them and hold pressure as told by the dispatcher. 7. Watch for shock and keep the person warm. Hands-on Stop the Bleed training makes packing far more effective.
source: Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons), as summarized in Florida DOH Stop the Bleed card

title: Tourniquet use for arm or leg bleeding
text: A tourniquet stops life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg when pressure isn't enough or can't be held (for example an amputation from a pipe or bucket). Steps: 1. Get help: Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) for anything serious. Make the scene safe. 2. Place the tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the bleeding site, between the wound and the heart. Don't place it on a joint (elbow or knee); go above the joint if needed. Over clothing is acceptable if it is not bulky. 3. Pull the strap as tight as you can and fasten it. 4. Twist the rod (windlass) until the bleeding stops. It will hurt; that is expected. Lock the windlass in its clip so it stays tight. 5. Note the time it went on; write it on the tourniquet or the person's skin and tell EMS. 6. Don't loosen or remove it. Only medical staff remove it. 7. If bleeding doesn't stop, Stop the Bleed training teaches placing a second tourniquet above the first. Use a commercial tourniquet if available; improvised ones (belt, rope) often fail. Keep one in every truck's kit.
source: Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons), as summarized in Florida DOH Stop the Bleed card; MedlinePlus traumatic amputation

title: Quick reference: locate color codes and tolerance zone
text: APWA locate colors: red electric; yellow gas, oil, steam; orange communications; blue potable water; purple reclaimed water and irrigation; green sewer and storm drain; white proposed excavation; pink temporary survey marks. Tolerance zone: commonly 18 inches each side of the marked facility or 24 inches, by state law; hand dig or vacuum excavate inside it. Typical notice: 2 to 3 business days (Iowa 48 hours excluding weekends and holidays). Tickets expire (Iowa: 25 calendar days after the wait period). Locators don't mark depth. Check your state's one-call law.
source: APWA color code; Iowa One Call manual

title: 811 call before you dig: how the process works
text: 811 is the national call-before-you-dig number; it routes to your state one-call center, which also takes online requests. Basic process: (1) pre-mark the dig area in white paint or flags (white lining) unless your state allows describing it; (2) contact 811 the required number of days ahead; (3) the center notifies member utilities, which send locators to mark their lines; (4) check responses (many states have a positive response system showing each utility's status); (5) respect the marks and dig carefully within the tolerance zone. Wait times vary by state: most require 2 to 3 business days' notice (Iowa: 48 hours, not counting weekends and holidays, starting at 6 am the next business day). Tickets expire (Iowa: 25 calendar days after the 48-hour wait), so renew for long jobs. Check your state's one-call law.
source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

title: Tolerance zone: hand digging near marked lines
text: The tolerance zone is the area on each side of a marked utility where mechanized digging isn't allowed, because marks are only approximate. Width depends on state law: many states use 18 inches either side of the outside edge of the utility, others 24 inches, and some use half the facility width plus 24 inches. Within the zone, expose the line by hand digging or vacuum excavation (or other nondestructive methods your state allows) to find its exact location and depth before digging nearby with a machine. Locators don't mark depth (Iowa's manual notes operators don't mark depth), so never assume a line is deep. Once exposed, support and protect it. Check your state's tolerance zone rule.
source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

title: Potholing and vacuum excavation
text: Potholing means digging a small test hole to expose a utility and confirm its exact location, depth, size and material. Vacuum excavation (hydro-excavation with water or air-excavation with compressed air, then vacuuming the spoil) is the preferred method near utilities because it's nondestructive and fast; many state laws recognize it as an acceptable method inside the tolerance zone. Tips: pothole every crossing utility ahead of the crew, ideally days ahead, so design conflicts get resolved before the crew arrives; record depth to top, size, material and station/offset; backfill and compact potholes per specs; use low water pressure near fragile lines and fiber; and remember hydro-excavation produces slurry that must be disposed of properly. Pothole data also supports change orders when utilities aren't where the plans show.
source: State one-call laws (e.g., Iowa One Call manual); common industry practice

title: White lining and good locate tickets
text: White lining means marking the proposed dig area with white paint, flags or stakes before calling 811, so locators know where to mark. Many states require it; a typical law requires white lining unless the location can be clearly described on the call or at a preconstruction meeting, electronic white-lining is used, or physical premarking is impractical (that is how the Iowa law puts it). Good tickets: give exact addresses and cross streets, describe the dig area (for example 'entire right of way, both sides of Main St from 1st Ave to 3rd Ave'), the type of work, depth and equipment, and the start date. Too-large tickets slow locates and may be rejected. Keep ticket numbers in the daily report and on site. Request re-marks when marks fade; Iowa's manual expects marks to last at least 5 working days on dirt and 10 on pavement.
source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

title: If you damage a utility line
text: If a line is hit or damaged, even a scrape, dent or nicked coating: For gas or hazardous liquid: stop work, shut off equipment if safe (one state one-call manual says in an emergency leave equipment where it is), evacuate people away and upwind, call 911, then the utility owner; don't try to stop the leak, don't operate switches or anything that can spark. For electric: stay away and keep others away; if on equipment touching a line, stay on it unless there's fire, then jump clear with feet together. For all damage: notify the utility owner as soon as practical with the type and extent, report to the one-call center where required, and don't backfill the area until the owner has inspected (unless they approve). Small coating damage on a steel gas line can cause corrosion leaks later, so report it. Document with photos and the ticket number.
source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

title: Emergency locates and working without marks
text: Most state one-call laws allow emergency excavation without waiting the normal notice period when there's a clear and immediate danger to life, health, essential services or significant property (a typical state definition), but you must still notify the one-call center as soon as practical and dig with extra care. Emergency tickets go to utilities immediately. Lack of marks is not permission to dig: if a utility hasn't responded by the end of the waiting period, check the positive response system and contact the utility; OSHA 1926.651(b)(2) only allows proceeding without a locate after 24 hours (or longer if state law says) with caution and detection equipment. Many states require you to wait for all responses. Abandoned lines and private lines (service lines past the meter, private electric, irrigation) aren't marked by 811 members; hire a private locator for those.
source: Iowa One Call Excavator Manual 2024

title: Can Ask classify trench soil from a photo? (No: the competent person does)
text: A photo can suggest what a soil probably is (clay, silt, sand, gravel, fill, organic, wet) and point out warning signs, but it cannot classify soil for trench safety. OSHA requires the competent person to classify soil as stable rock, Type A, B or C using at least one visual and at least one manual test on site, for example a thumb penetration, plasticity or dry strength test, or a pocket penetrometer or shear vane, and to reclassify when conditions change (rain, seepage, vibration, drying, cracking). Ask will never say a trench is safe, unsafe, Type A, B or C, or OK to enter from a picture. What Ask can do: describe what the photo appears to show, list the on-site tests the competent person may run, and flag things to point out to them, such as cracks, seepage, layers, old backfill or sloughing.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401

title: What clay looks like in a trench wall and spoil pile
text: Clay in a trench wall usually cuts clean and smooth, often leaving a shiny, polished face where the bucket teeth dragged. Colors run gray, blue-gray, brown, red, yellow or mottled. Spoil comes out in solid chunks and slabs with sharp edges rather than crumbling, and sticks to the bucket, boots and tires. Dry clay crusts and shrinks into blocky clods with cracks (desiccation cracks); dry clods are hard to break by hand. Wet clay is slick, sticky and glossy and holds footprints with smooth sides. In the OSHA visual test, soil that stays in clumps when excavated is cohesive. Look-alikes: silt (dull face, crumbles, dusty dry, gets soupy when shaken), wet sandy clay (gritty), fill with clay lumps. Feel tests (ribbon, thread, dry strength) narrow it down; classification for shoring is the competent person's call.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

title: Clay by feel: ribbon, shine, sticky and the thread test
text: Hand tests for clay (USDA texture by feel and OSHA manual tests): Wet a walnut-size lump to putty consistency and squeeze it between thumb and forefinger into a ribbon. Per USDA NRCS, a ribbon under 1 in is weak, about 1 to 2 in is moderate, and 2 in or longer is strong; strong ribbons that feel smooth mean clay, gritty ones mean sandy clay. Rub a wet pinch: clay feels sticky and smooth and leaves a shine when you rub it with a thumbnail or knife blade. OSHA's plasticity test: roll a moist sample into threads about 1/8 in diameter; if a 2 in thread can be held by one end without tearing, the soil is cohesive. Dry strength: dry clay lumps break only with real force. These tests describe the soil; they do not by themselves set the OSHA soil type, which also depends on strength, fissures, water and history.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: USDA NRCS Soil Quality Test Kit Guide, ch. 11 Soil texture by feel; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401

title: Clay vs silt vs fine sand: a 60 second field check
text: Take a handful of moist soil. Look: can you see individual grains? Yes means sand. Rub wet: gritty means sand, floury-smooth means silt, sticky-smooth means clay. Ribbon: clay makes a long ribbon (2 in or more is strong per USDA texture by feel), silt barely ribbons, sand will not. Shake a wet pat: water rises fast in silt and fine sand, nothing happens in clay. Dry a lump on the dash or in the sun: clay dries hard and needs force to break, silt crumbles to powder, sand falls apart. Wash your hands: sand rinses off, silt rinses easily, clay smears and needs scrubbing. Most soils are mixes (sandy clay, silty sand), so describe the main part first. Never taste or bite soil near sewer or contaminated work. Classification for protective systems is the competent person's job.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: USDA NRCS Soil Quality Test Kit Guide, ch. 11 Soil texture by feel; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

title: What sand looks like in a trench wall (grains, runs, dries pale)
text: Sand in a trench wall shows visible grains, usually tan, gray, yellow, orange or white, often in layers with slightly different colors. Clean sand does not hold together: spoil falls into a loose pile with smooth sloping sides and no chunks. Damp sand may hold a near-vertical face briefly because of moisture, then the face dries pale from the top and starts to dribble or ravel; a ledge of sand at the toe of the wall or a slope of fallen grains shows the face is moving. Wet, running sand flows into the trench and can boil up from the bottom where water is pushing in. OSHA's visual test treats soil that breaks up easily and does not hold together as granular. Look-alikes: silt (no visible grains, floury), sandy fill with debris. Classification and protective system are set by the competent person on site.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

title: What fissured clay looks like (cracks, blocky, slick planes)
text: OSHA defines fissured soil as material that tends to break along definite planes of fracture with little resistance, or that shows open cracks such as tension cracks on an exposed surface. In a trench wall it looks like clay broken into blocks or wedges by thin cracks, sometimes with shiny, polished, grooved faces (slickensides) where the blocks slid against each other, often in old expansive clays. Spoil breaks into angular blocks along those cracks rather than tearing. OSHA's drying test: dry a sample about 1 in thick and 6 in across; cracks during drying indicate significant fissures, and dry clumps that break easily into smaller clumps indicate fissured material. Fissured clay can drop blocks without warning. A photo may show cracks, but the competent person decides whether the soil is fissured and what that means for the protective system.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401

title: Previously disturbed soil vs undisturbed ground: what to look for
text: OSHA treats previously disturbed soil as unable to be Type A, so spotting it matters to the competent person. Undisturbed native ground usually shows consistent layers that run level or follow the land, natural color changes, roots that thin with depth, and a firm, uniform face. Disturbed soil (old trench backfill, fill, utility crossings) shows: mixed colors in lumps and swirls, chunks of different soils jumbled together, sharp vertical boundaries (the edge of an old trench), loose or softer zones, sand or gravel bedding, warning tape, old pipes, concrete or asphalt pieces, bricks, trash, or a different smell. Water often seeps along old trench lines. In a photo, an old trench often shows as a rectangle or V of different-colored soil in the wall. Point it out to the competent person; the call is theirs.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

title: Layered soils in a trench wall: what layers look like and why they matter
text: Layers show as bands of different color or texture across the trench wall: sand over clay, gravel lenses, silt seams, peat bands. OSHA's visual test asks the competent person to examine layers and judge whether they slope toward the excavation and how steeply. Things to look for: a weaker layer (sand, silt, gravel) under a stiffer one, which can undercut and drop the layer above; water seeping out at the top of a clay layer (a perched water line, often with orange staining); layers dipping toward the trench; thin slick seams. In a photo, use a tape or rod in the shot to show depth and thickness. OSHA's rule for layered systems is that the soil is classified by the weakest layer in many cases; that classification is the competent person's job, done on site.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

title: What saturated or seeping soil looks like in a trench
text: Signs of water in a trench wall or bottom: dark, glistening wet bands or patches on the face; water weeping, dripping or trickling from a layer; small fans of washed sand or silt at the toe; a muddy pool or standing water in the bottom; soft, pumping ground under a compactor; sand boiling or bubbling up from the bottom; sloughing or slumping of the wall below a wet zone; and spoil that slumps and runs. OSHA's visual test includes looking for surface water, water seeping from the sides and the water table level, and the soil classification must be revised when the excavation gets wet. Submerged or freely seeping soil generally cannot be treated as Type A or B. Tell the competent person right away; dewatering and protective changes are their call. Ask cannot say a wet trench is safe.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

title: Warning signs in a trench photo to point out to the competent person
text: OSHA's visual test lists what the competent person looks for, and these are worth pointing out if they show in a photo: tension cracks parallel to the trench edge back from the top; chunks spalling off the vertical face, which can mean fissuring or moving ground; bulging, sloughing or a toe of fallen soil; layers that slope toward the trench; water on the surface, seeping from the walls, or standing in the bottom; utilities, old structures or signs of previously disturbed soil; vibration sources such as traffic or equipment near the edge; and spoil or equipment too close to the edge (OSHA requires spoil at least 2 ft back). Ask can describe these from a photo, but it cannot decide whether the trench is safe or what protective system is needed. Stop and get the competent person if you see them.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.651(j)(2) (spoil at least 2 ft from the edge)

title: Spoil pile clues: what the dirt coming out tells you
text: OSHA's visual test includes watching samples and spoil as they are dug. Clues: soil that comes out in clumps and holds together is cohesive; soil that falls apart and runs is granular; mostly fine-grained material points to cohesive soil, coarse sand or gravel to granular. Other spoil clues: big blocky slabs that break along shiny cracks suggest fissured clay; mixed colors, trash, brick or asphalt mean previously disturbed fill; wet, flowing spoil that spreads flat means saturated silt or sand; black, smelly spoil points to organics or contamination; white hard lumps in dry country point to caliche. Change from one kind of spoil to another tells you the ground changed and the classification may need to change. Report changes to the competent person; they run the manual tests.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401; General industry and supplier practice (appearance varies by quarry and region)

title: Thumb penetration and pocket penetrometer: what they are (not a photo test)
text: The thumb penetration test is one of OSHA's manual tests for cohesive soil. As OSHA describes it, a Type A soil (unconfined strength about 1.5 tons per square foot) can be indented by the thumb only with great effort, while a Type C soil (about 0.5 tsf) can be penetrated several inches by the thumb and molded by light finger pressure. The test is done on an undisturbed clump as soon as it is dug, and the soil must be rechecked if it gets wet. A pocket penetrometer or hand shear vane gives a number for the same idea. These tests need the soil in hand, done by the competent person. A photo of someone's thumb in a soil face does not tell Ask the soil type, because the force used and the condition of the sample are unknown.
topic: Visual ID: soils by eye and hand
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix A (soil classification visual and manual tests), as adopted in WAC 296-155-66401

title: Trench backfill slurry and CLSM
text: Slurry (sand-cement trench backfill) and CLSM (controlled low-strength material, flowable fill) fill a trench without compaction: good for narrow trenches, around tight utilities and when the agency wants quick paving. Greenbook covers trench backfill slurry in 201-1 and CLSM in 201-6; agencies often call out a sack content (like 1-sack or 2-sack slurry) and a maximum strength so it can be dug again later. Place it in lifts if the pipe can float, block or weight the pipe, and keep it off fresh joints until set. Slurry is cut back below the pavement surface before the final paving (Greenbook: 1 to 8 in).
source: Greenbook 201-1, 201-6, 306-12.2 (California)

title: T-cut and paving a trench
text: Typical city trench repair: sawcut the existing pavement straight and clean, compact the backfill and base, then sawcut back beyond each trench wall (a T-cut, often 12 in each side) so the new asphalt bears on undisturbed base; tack the edges; pave at least the existing thickness or thicker (Greenbook: 1 in thicker than existing) in compacted lifts; roll to 95 percent; finish flush with the existing street. Temporary paving (cold patch or hot mix, at least 2 in) holds until permanent paving. Many cities also require crack seal on the joints, restriping and a final grind and overlay when several trenches are close. Steel plates over open trenches need ramps or recessing and a pin-down, per the agency.
source: Greenbook 306-13; typical city trench repair standards (California)
